claim: The tips of the developing respiratory buds are home to important progenitor cells marked by the expression of SOX9 and ID2.
source: The tips of the developing respiratory buds are home to important progenitor cells marked by the expression of SOX9 and ID2.
evidence: Supported by citations to Rawlins et al., 2009 and Morrisey and Hogan, 2010

claim: Early in embryonic development (prior to E13.5), SOX9+ progenitors are multipotent, generating both airway and alveolar epithelium.
source: Early in embryonic development (prior to E13.5), SOX9+progenitors are multipotent, generating both airway and alveolar epithelium, but are selective progenitors of alveolar epithelial cells later in development.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies including Rawlins et al., 2009; Laresgoiti et al., 2016; Nichane et al., 2017; Nikolić et al., 2017

claim: SOX9+ progenitors are selective progenitors of alveolar epithelial cells later in development.
source: Early in embryonic development (prior to E13.5), SOX9+progenitors are multipotent, generating both airway and alveolar epithelium, but are selective progenitors of alveolar epithelial cells later in development.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Transcription factors including Sox9, Etv5, Irx, Mycn, and Foxp1/2 interact in complex gene regulatory networks to control proliferation and differentiation of SOX9+ progenitors.
source: Transcription factors, including Sox9, Etv5, Irx, Mycn, and Foxp1/2 interact in complex gene regulatory networks to control proliferation and differentiation of SOX9+progenitors.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Widespread changes in chromatin accessibility were observed between E11.5 and E16.5 in SOX9+ epithelial progenitor cells.
source: Widespread changes in chromatin accessibility were observed between E11.5 and E16.5, particularly at distal cis-regulatory elements (e.g. enhancers).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-Seq data presented in the manuscript

claim: Changes in chromatin accessibility between E11.5 and E16.5 occurred particularly at distal cis-regulatory elements (e.g. enhancers).
source: Widespread changes in chromatin accessibility were observed between E11.5 and E16.5, particularly at distal cis-regulatory elements (e.g. enhancers).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-Seq data showing preferential changes outside promoter regions

claim: Gene regulatory network inference identified phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) signaling in the developmental regulation of SOX9+ progenitor cells.
source: Gene regulatory network (GRN) inference identified a common SOX9+ progenitor GRN, implicating phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) signaling in the developmental regulation of SOX9+ progenitor cells.
evidence: Supported by PECA computational modeling and ATAC-Seq/RNA-Seq data

claim: Conditional ablation of PI3K signaling in the developing lung epithelium in mouse resulted in an expansion of the SOX9+ EPC population.
source: Consistent with this model, conditional ablation of PI3K signaling in the developing lung epithelium in mouse resulted in an expansion of the SOX9+ EPC population and impaired airway epithelial cell differentiation.
evidence: Supported by in vivo genetic experiments using Shh-Cre x Pik3caf/f mice

claim: Conditional ablation of PI3K signaling in the developing lung epithelium in mouse resulted in impaired airway epithelial cell differentiation.
source: Consistent with this model, conditional ablation of PI3K signaling in the developing lung epithelium in mouse resulted in an expansion of the SOX9+ EPC population and impaired airway epithelial cell differentiation.
evidence: Supported by in vivo genetic experiments showing decreased secretory and ciliated cells

claim: PI3K signaling is required for epithelial patterning during lung organogenesis.
source: These data demonstrate that PI3K signaling is required for epithelial patterning during lung organogenesis, and emphasize the combinatorial power of paired RNA and ATAC seq in defining regulatory networks in development.
evidence: Supported by genetic ablation experiments and phenotypic analysis

claim: Morphogenesis of the mammalian lung begins as an outpouching of a simple bud from the embryonic foregut.
source: Morphogenesis of the mammalian lung begins as an outpouching of a simple bud from the embryonic foregut, which branches and extends into the splanchnic mesoderm as the primitive respiratory tubules are formed.
evidence: Established knowledge in developmental biology

claim: The tips of the lung bud are lined by highly proliferative epithelial progenitor cells marked by expression of the genes Sox9 and Id2.
source: The tips of the lung bud are lined by highly proliferative epithelial progenitor cells marked by expression of the genes Sox9 and Id2 (Rawlins et al., 2009; Morrisey and Hogan, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rawlins et al., 2009 and Morrisey and Hogan, 2010

claim: Over the course of early lung development, SOX9+ progenitor cells give rise to the entire complement of lung epithelium, from proximal airway epithelial cells to distal type I (AT1) and type II alveolar (AT2) epithelial cells.
source: Over the course of early lung development, SOX9+ progenitor cells give rise to the entire complement of lung epithelium, from proximal airway epithelial cells to distal type I (AT1) and type II alveolar (AT2) epithelial cells (Rawlins et al., 2009; Laresgoiti et al., 2016; Nichane et al., 2017; Nikolić et al., 2017; Miller et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Chromatin state serves as a medium through which various developmental and external stimuli are integrated into comprehensive cellular programs.
source: Chromatin state serves as a medium through which various developmental and external stimuli are integrated into comprehensive cellular programs which enable regulatory proteins access to activate or repress gene expression.
evidence: Established concept in epigenetics

claim: Epigenetic programs controlling progenitor cell identities are maintained in spite of repeated rounds of cellular division, fluctuating transcription factor levels, or dynamic inputs from various signaling pathways.
source: Epigenetic programs controlling progenitor cell identies are maintained in spite of repeated rounds of cellular division, fluctuating transcription factor levels, or dynamic inputs from various signaling pathways, (Klemm et al., 2019; Sheikh and Akhtar, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Klemm et al., 2019 and Sheikh and Akhtar, 2019

claim: Chromatin accessibility changes dynamically throughout development to establish and maintain cellular identity in a variety of cell types and organ systems.
source: Chromatin accessibility changes dynamically throughout development, to establish and maintain cellular identity in a variety of cell types and organ systems (Gorkin et al., 2017; Trevino et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gorkin et al., 2017 and Trevino et al., 2020

claim: Accessible chromatin regions only make up a minority of the genome (2–3%).
source: Although accessible chromatin regions only make up a minority of the genome (2–3%), they account for a high proportion of the genomic loci bound by transcription factors, and are highly correlated with cis-regulatory elements (CREs) identified by other methods, such as promoters, enhancers, insulators, and silencers (Buenrostro et al., 2013; Buenrostro et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buenrostro et al., 2013 and 2015b

claim: Accessible chromatin regions account for a high proportion of the genomic loci bound by transcription factors.
source: Although accessible chromatin regions only make up a minority of the genome (2–3%), they account for a high proportion of the genomic loci bound by transcription factors, and are highly correlated with cis-regulatory elements (CREs) identified by other methods, such as promoters, enhancers, insulators, and silencers (Buenrostro et al., 2013; Buenrostro et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buenrostro et al., 2013 and 2015b

claim: Accessible chromatin regions are highly correlated with cis-regulatory elements (CREs) identified by other methods, such as promoters, enhancers, insulators, and silencers.
source: Although accessible chromatin regions only make up a minority of the genome (2–3%), they account for a high proportion of the genomic loci bound by transcription factors, and are highly correlated with cis-regulatory elements (CREs) identified by other methods, such as promoters, enhancers, insulators, and silencers (Buenrostro et al., 2013; Buenrostro et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buenrostro et al., 2013 and 2015b

claim: Accessible chromatin regions in SOX9+ cells were highly correlated with lung-specific histone post-translational modifications (PTMs) found on validated cis-regulatory elements.
source: Acessible chromatin regions in SOX9+ cells were highly correlated with lung-specific histone post-translational modifications (PTMs) found on validated cis-regulatory elements.
evidence: Supported by comparison with ENCODE ChIP-Seq data for H3K4me3, H3K4me1, and H3K27ac

claim: Dynamic changes in accessible chromatin regions were correlated with gene expression changes observed during the course of SOX9+ lung epithelial cell differentiation.
source: Dynamic changes in these accessible chromatin regions were correlated with gene expression changes observed during the course of SOX9+ lung epithelial cell differeniation.
evidence: Supported by paired RNA-Seq and ATAC-Seq analysis

claim: Chromatin accessibility changes were observed in or near genes associated with phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) signaling.
source: Chromatin accessibility changes were observed in or near genes associated with phophatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) signaling.
evidence: Supported by ATAC-Seq data and gene ontology analysis

claim: Genetic ablation of PI3K signaling within the lung epithelium caused expansion of the SOX9+ progenitor cell population at the expense of mature lung epithelial cell differentiation.
source: Genetic ablation of PI3K signaling within the lung epithelium caused expansion of the SOX9+ progenitor cell population at the expense of mature lung epithelial cell differentiation.
evidence: Supported by in vivo experiments using Pik3ca cKO mice

claim: Shortly after lung specification occurs, highly proliferative distal progenitor cells marked by the expression of SOX9+ appear at the tips of the growing lung buds.
source: Shortly after lung specification occurs, highly proliferative distal progenitor cells marked by the expression of SOX9+ appear at the tips of the growing lung buds (Figure 1A–I).
evidence: Supported by whole mount confocal imaging and immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 1

claim: A suite of transcription factors (eg, Id2, Etv5, Foxp1/2, Mycn) play critical roles in the development of the SOX9+ distal tip progenitor cell population.
source: A suite of transcription factors (eg, Id2, Etv5, Foxp1/2, Mycn) play critical roles in the development of the SOX9+ distal tip progenitor cell population (Figure 1D; Morrisey and Hogan, 2010; Swarr and Morrisey, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morrisey and Hogan, 2010 and Swarr and Morrisey, 2015

claim: Pseudotime analysis of RNA-Seq data from mouse lung epithelium from E11.5 to E16.5 shows two distinct pseudotime branches arising from SOX9+ progenitors, terminating in airway and distal lung epithelial cells at E16.5.
source: Starting from E11.5, two distinct pseudotime branches arise from SOX9+ progenitors, terminating in airway and distal lung epithelial cells at E16.5 (Figure 1J–K, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by Monocle pseudotime analysis of RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1

claim: Monocle analysis revealed 26 unique gene modules consisting of co-regulated genes during distal differentiation.
source: We used Monocle to find modules consisting of co-regulated genes during distal differentiation, revealing 26 unique gene modules.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of RNA-Seq data

claim: Gene module 8 consists of genes highly expressed at E11.5 lung and preserved in the distal differential branch, including Sox9, Wnt7b, Bmp4, and Hmga2.
source: One such gene module consists of genes highly expressed E11.5 lung and preserved the distal differential branch of the Monocle pseudotime analysis; these genes are involved in lung epithelial development and early branching, including Sox9, Wnt7b, Bmp4, and Hmga2, validating the significance of both the pseudotime analyses and gene module predictions while also identifying other coordinately expressed genes that may be involved in EPC differentiation (module 8, Figure 1L–M).
evidence: Supported by Monocle gene module analysis shown in Figure 1L-M

claim: More than 34,000 regions of open chromatin were identified by ATAC-Seq at E11.5 and E16.5.
source: Analysis of chromatin accessibility by ATAC-Seq identified over 30,000 regions of open chromatin at each timepoint (E11.5, n=34,602; E16.5, n=40,823; Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by ATAC-Seq peak calling data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The genome-wide distribution of ATAC-Seq peaks was consistent with previously published chromatin accessibility studies, showing a high-degree of enrichment near gene transcriptional start sites (TSS).
source: The genome-wide distribution of ATAC-Seq peaks was consistent with previously published chromatin accessibility studies, showing a high-degree of enrichment near gene transcriptional start sites (TSS) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C-H).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C-H

claim: The presence of ATAC-Seq peaks positively correlated with expression of the nearest gene.
source: The presence of ATAC-Seq peaks positively correlated with expression the nearest gene (RNA-Seq), and this correlation was strongest for peaks within promoter regions.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between ATAC-Seq and RNA-Seq data

claim: The correlation between ATAC-Seq peaks and gene expression was strongest for peaks within promoter regions.
source: The presence of ATAC-Seq peaks positively correlated with expression the nearest gene (RNA-Seq), and this correlation was strongest for peaks within promoter regions.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between ATAC-Seq and RNA-Seq data

claim: Peaks only detected at a single developmental timepoint were associated with higher levels of expression of the nearest gene at that same developmental stage.
source: Moreover, peaks only detected at a single developmental timepoint were associated with higher levels of expression of the nearst gene at that same developmental stage (for example, genes nearest to peaks unique to the E11.5 developmental stage overall were observed to have higher expression levels at E11.5 compared to E16.5; Figure 2E–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A-E).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2E-F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A-E

claim: Significant enrichment was observed for H3K4me3 read density across peaks predicted to reside within gene promoter regions.
source: Significant enrichment was observed for H3K4me3 read density (cluster 1, as identified through unbiased hierarchial clustering) across peaks predicted to reside within gene promoter regions (Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 4F, G).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 2C-D

claim: A subset of ATAC-Seq peaks (cluster 2) were enriched for either both H3K4me1 and H3K27ac read density, or H3K4me1 read density alone, consistent with an 'active' or 'decommissioned' enhancer states, respectively.
source: A second subset of ATAC-Seq peaks (cluster 2) were enriched for either both H3K4me1 and H3K27ac read density, or H3K4me1 ready density alone, consistent with an 'active' or 'decommissioned' enhancer states, respectively (Jadhav et al., 2019). (Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 4F, G)
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq data analysis and citation to Jadhav et al., 2019

claim: Regions identified by ATAC-Seq represent a bona fide map of active cis-regulatory elements (e.g. promoters, active and decommissioned enhancers) within the SOX9+ lung epithelial progenitor cells.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that regions identified by ATAC-Seq represent a bona fide map of active cis-regulatory elements (e.g. promoters, active and decommissioned enhancers) within the SOX9+ lung epithelial progenitor cells, and that these regulatory elements are regulating the transcriptional dynamics observed during EPC development.
evidence: Inferred from correlation with histone marks and gene expression

claim: Nearly a quarter of accessible chromatin regions were unique to each developmental timepoint (E11.5 and E16.5).
source: Nearly a quarter of accessible chromatin regions were unique to each developmental timepoint, a remarkable observation given that the two cell populations are SOX9+ lung epithelial progenitor cells separated by just 5 days of development (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-Seq peak comparison analysis

claim: 18,582 regions of chromatin were more accessible at E11.5 (E11.5-DARs).
source: We used the MACS2 bdgdiff tool to identify regions of chromatin that were more accessible at E11.5 (n=18,582), more accessible at E16.5 (n=11,980), or did not undergo significant changes in accessibility between the two timepoints (n=35,312) (hereafter referred to as E11.5-differentially accessible regions (DARs), E16.5-DARs, and common regions, respectively).
evidence: Supported by MACS2 bdgdiff analysis of ATAC-Seq data

claim: 11,980 regions of chromatin were more accessible at E16.5 (E16.5-DARs).
source: We used the MACS2 bdgdiff tool to identify regions of chromatin that were more accessible at E11.5 (n=18,582), more accessible at E16.5 (n=11,980), or did not undergo significant changes in accessibility between the two timepoints (n=35,312) (hereafter referred to as E11.5-differentially accessible regions (DARs), E16.5-DARs, and common regions, respectively).
evidence: Supported by MACS2 bdgdiff analysis of ATAC-Seq data

claim: 35,312 regions did not undergo significant changes in accessibility between E11.5 and E16.5 (common regions).
source: We used the MACS2 bdgdiff tool to identify regions of chromatin that were more accessible at E11.5 (n=18,582), more accessible at E16.5 (n=11,980), or did not undergo significant changes in accessibility between the two timepoints (n=35,312) (hereafter referred to as E11.5-differentially accessible regions (DARs), E16.5-DARs, and common regions, respectively).
evidence: Supported by MACS2 bdgdiff analysis of ATAC-Seq data

claim: Compared to peaks that did not undergo changes in chromatin accessibility, DARs were significantly more likely to be found within intronic and intergenic regions.
source: However, compared to peaks that did not undergo changes in chromatin accessibility, DARs were significantly more likely to be found within intronic and intergenic regions, and were less likely to be found within promoters (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 4I).
evidence: Supported by genomic location analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: DARs were less likely to be found within promoters compared to peaks that did not undergo changes in chromatin accessibility.
source: However, compared to peaks that did not undergo changes in chromatin accessibility, DARs were significantly more likely to be found within intronic and intergenic regions, and were less likely to be found within promoters (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 4I).
evidence: Supported by genomic location analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: DARs at both E11.5 and E16.5 exhibited peak H3K4me1 read density in close proximity to the center of the DAR.
source: DARs at both E11.5 and E16.5 exhibited peak H3K4me1 read density in close proximity to the center of the DAR.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq read density analysis

claim: There was relative de-enrichment of H3K4me1 read density at the center of common regions.
source: In contrast, there was relative de-enrichment of H3K4me1 read density at the center of common regions (and peaks flanking the common region by ~500 bp on each side) (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq read density analysis shown in Figure 2H

claim: Read density for the promoter mark H3K4me3 was significantly enriched and centered on common region peaks, compared to DAR peaks.
source: Similarly, read density for the promoter mark H3K4me3 was significantly enriched and centered on common region peaks, compared to DAR peaks (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-Seq read density analysis shown in Figure 2I

claim: At the genome-wide level, changes in chromatin accessibility were significantly correlated with differential gene expression.
source: At the genome-wide level, changes in chromatin accessibility were significantly correlated with differential gene expression.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between ATAC-Seq and RNA-Seq data

claim: Genes adjacent to regions of chromatin more accessible at E11.5 (E11.5-DARs) were significantly more likely to have higher mRNA expression at E11.5 compared to E16.5.
source: Genes adjacent to regions of chromatin more accessible at E11.5 (E11.5-DARs) were significantly more likely to have higher mRNA expression at E11.5 compared to E16.5, and vice versa (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2J

claim: Genes adjacent to regions of chromatin more accessible at E16.5 (E16.5-DARs) were significantly more likely to have higher mRNA expression at E16.5 compared to E11.5.
source: Genes adjacent to regions of chromatin more accessible at E11.5 (E11.5-DARs) were significantly more likely to have higher mRNA expression at E11.5 compared to E16.5, and vice versa (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2J

claim: Developmental changes in chromatin accessibility were preferentially located outside of the promoter regions at distal cis-regulatory elements (e.g. enhancers).
source: Moreover, although chromatin remodeling occurs across all types of cis-regulatory elements during development of SOX9+lung epithelial progenitors, developmental changes in chromatin accessibility were preferentially located outside of the promoter regions at distal cis-regulatory elements (e.g. enhancers).
evidence: Inferred from genomic location analysis of DARs

claim: Chromatin accessibility at distal CREs such as enhancers likely plays a key and incompletely explored role in directing lung epithelial development.
source: Collectively, these data also emphasize that chromatin accessibility at distal CREs such as enchancers likely plays a key and incompletely explored role in directing lung epithelial development.
evidence: Inferred from the preferential location of DARs at distal elements

claim: The PECA computational model was used to build a gene regulatory network for the SOX9+ EPC population at E11.5 and E16.5.
source: To this end, we used the Paired Expression and Chromatin Accessibility (PECA) computational model to build a gene regulatory network for the SOX9+ EPC population at E11.5 and E16.5 (Duren et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duren et al., 2017 and application of the PECA model

claim: Well-studied transcription factors, including Id2, Irx and Foxp factors, Etv5, and Foxa2 appear as central nodes in the SOX9+ progenitor gene regulatory network.
source: Well-studied transcription factors, including those highlighted in Figure 1D, such as Id2, Irx and Foxp factors, Etv5, and Foxa2 appear as central nodes.
evidence: Supported by PECA gene regulatory network analysis

claim: Several key nodes in the SOX9+ progenitor gene regulatory network have previously been shown to interface with the PI3K signaling pathway.
source: Intriguingly, several of these key nodes have previously shown to interface with the PI3K signaling pathway (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: Supported by literature citations and network analysis shown in Figure 3D-G

claim: The transcription factor Sox4 has been implicated in the pathogenesis of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
source: The transcription factor Sox4, which has been implicated in the pathogenesis of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and was recently found to be enriched in a regeneration associated pre-alveolar type-1 cell transitional state (PATS), has been shown to both regulate and have its own expression regulated by PI3K signaling (Ramezani-Rad et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2019; Bilir et al., 2016; Mehta et al., 2017; Kobayashi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Sox4 was recently found to be enriched in a regeneration associated pre-alveolar type-1 cell transitional state (PATS).
source: The transcription factor Sox4, which has been implicated in the pathogenesis of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and was recently found to be enriched in a regeneration associated pre-alveolar type-1 cell transitional state (PATS), has been shown to both regulate and have its own expression regulated by PI3K signaling (Ramezani-Rad et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2019; Bilir et al., 2016; Mehta et al., 2017; Kobayashi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Sox4 has been shown to both regulate and have its own expression regulated by PI3K signaling.
source: The transcription factor Sox4, which has been implicated in the pathogenesis of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and was recently found to be enriched in a regeneration associated pre-alveolar type-1 cell transitional state (PATS), has been shown to both regulate and have its own expression regulated by PI3K signaling (Ramezani-Rad et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2019; Bilir et al., 2016; Mehta et al., 2017; Kobayashi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ramezani-Rad et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2019; Bilir et al., 2016; Mehta et al., 2017; Kobayashi et al., 2020

claim: Hbp1 is a known repressor of beta-catenin transactivation.
source: Another central node in this network, Hbp1, is a known repressor of beta-catenin transactivation, but is also negatively regulated by PI3K signaling (Coomans de Brachène et al., 2014; Bollaert et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Coomans de Brachène et al., 2014 and Bollaert et al., 2018

claim: Hbp1 is negatively regulated by PI3K signaling.
source: Another central node in this network, Hbp1, is a known repressor of beta-catenin transactivation, but is also negatively regulated by PI3K signaling (Coomans de Brachène et al., 2014; Bollaert et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Coomans de Brachène et al., 2014 and Bollaert et al., 2018

claim: Grhl2 promotes airway differentiation in the lung.
source: Finally, Grhl2, a third central node in this network, was predicted to be regulated via the PI3K signaling component Pten. Previous work has shown Ghrl2 promotes airway differentiation in the lung, and that loss of Grhl2 in the lung leads to expansion of the SOX9+ EPC population (Kersbergen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kersbergen et al., 2018

claim: Loss of Grhl2 in the lung leads to expansion of the SOX9+ EPC population.
source: Finally, Grhl2, a third central node in this network, was predicted to be regulated via the PI3K signaling component Pten. Previous work has shown Ghrl2 promotes airway differentiation in the lung, and that loss of Grhl2 in the lung leads to expansion of the SOX9+ EPC population (Kersbergen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kersbergen et al., 2018

claim: Grhl2 was predicted to be regulated via the PI3K signaling component Pten.
source: Finally, Grhl2, a third central node in this network, was predicted to be regulated via the PI3K signaling component Pten.
evidence: Predicted by PECA gene regulatory network analysis

claim: Analysis of ATAC-Seq data identified activation of a number of signaling pathways that were less apparent by RNA analysis alone.
source: While similar biological processes were enriched in both the ATAC-Seq and RNA-Seq data, analysis of ATAC-Seq data identified activation of a number of signaling pathways that were less apparent by RNA analysis alone.
evidence: Supported by comparison of GSEA results from ATAC-Seq and RNA-Seq data

claim: Analysis of ATAC-Seq data identified a potential role for cAMP, Rap1, Ras, MAPK, TGF-beta, and PI3K-mTOR signaling in the development and differentiation of the SOX9+ lung epithelial progenitor cells.
source: However, analysis ATAC-Seq data identified a potential role for a number of additional pathways in the development and differentiation of the SOX9+ lung epithelial progenitor cells, including cAMP, Rap1, Ras, MAPK, TGF-beta, and, importantly, PI3K-mTOR signaling (Figure 4A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Supported by GSEA of ATAC-Seq data shown in Figure 4A-C

claim: Genes nearest to increasingly accessible regions of chromatin (E16.5-DARs) as EPC maturation proceeded were most strongly enriched in genes associated with phosphatidylinositol (KEGG mmu04070) and PI3K signaling (KEGG mmu04151).
source: Consistent with both the PECA and GSEA analyses, genes nearest to increasingly accessible regions of chromatin (E16.5-DARs) as EPC maturation proceeded were most strongly enriched in genes associated with phosphatidylinositol (KEGG mmu04070) and PI3K signaling (KEGG mmu04151).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis of genes near E16.5-DARs

claim: Genes nearest to common accessible regions were significantly enriched in phosphatidylinositol and PI3K signaling pathways.
source: Genes nearest to common accessible regions were also significantly enriched in these same pathways (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: Components of the PI3K signaling pathway (eg. Pik3ca, Pikap1, Pik3r1, Pten), upstream ligand/receptors (eg. Egfr, Fgf1, Igf1r) and known downstream targets of PI3K signaling were associated with common accessible regions and E16.5 DARs.
source: Components of the PI3K signaling pathway (eg. Pik3ca, Pikap1, Pik3r1, Pten), upstream ligand/receptors (eg. Egfr, Fgf1, Igf1r) and known downstream targets of PI3K signaling were associated with common accessible regions and E16.5 DARs (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Supported by analysis of genes near accessible regions shown in Figure 4D-F

claim: Expression of many core PI3K pathway components did not change between E11.5 and E16.5.
source: While expression of many of core pathway components did not change between E11.5 and E16.5, expression of a number of potential upstream receptor/ligands (e.g. Igfr, Fgf1) and downstream targets of PI3K signaling increased, including major components of the epithelial basement membrane (e.g. Lama3, Col4a3).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq expression data

claim: Expression of a number of potential upstream receptor/ligands (e.g. Igfr, Fgf1) and downstream targets of PI3K signaling increased between E11.5 and E16.5.
source: While expression of many of core pathway components did not change between E11.5 and E16.5, expression of a number of potential upstream receptor/ligands (e.g. Igfr, Fgf1) and downstream targets of PI3K signaling increased, including major components of the epithelial basement membrane (e.g. Lama3, Col4a3).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq expression data

claim: The highest levels of pAKT expression, and PI3K pathway activation, were observed in the proximal lung epithelium as early as E12.5.
source: The highest levels of pAKT expression, and PI3K pathway activation, were observed in the proximal lung epithelium as early as E12.5 (Figure 5A–C) and persisted in the airway epithelium through adulthood (Figure 5J–L).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy for pAKT shown in Figure 5

claim: High levels of pAKT expression persisted in the airway epithelium through adulthood.
source: The highest levels of pAKT expression, and PI3K pathway activation, were observed in the proximal lung epithelium as early as E12.5 (Figure 5A–C) and persisted in the airway epithelium through adulthood (Figure 5J–L).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy for pAKT shown in Figure 5J-L

claim: Early in development (E12.5) pAKT was more broadly expressed throughout the lung epithelium, with a 'bimodal' pattern of distribution, with high expression levels in the proximal epithelium and a second peak of signal intensity at the distal branch tips.
source: Interestingly, early in development (E12.5) pAKT was more broadly expressed throughout the lung epithelium, and there appear to be a 'bimodal' pattern of distribution, with high expression levels in the proximal epithelium and a second peak of signal intensity at the distal branch tips.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy for pAKT

claim: Much lower levels of pAKT expression and PI3K activation were observed in the mesenchyme at all ages.
source: Much lower levels of pAKT expression and PI3K activation were observed in the mesenchyme at all ages, and the distal lung epithelium at later stages of development (Figure 5D–L).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy for pAKT shown in Figure 5D-L

claim: Much lower levels of pAKT expression and PI3K activation were observed in the distal lung epithelium at later stages of development.
source: Much lower levels of pAKT expression and PI3K activation were observed in the mesenchyme at all ages, and the distal lung epithelium at later stages of development (Figure 5D–L).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy for pAKT shown in Figure 5D-L

claim: A proximal-to-distal gradient of PI3K signaling within the lung epithelium may be required for lung epithelial differentiation and proper establishment of epithelial cell-type identity.
source: These data support the concept that a proximal-to-distal gradient of PI3K signaling within the lung epithelium may be required for lung epithelial differentiation and proper establishment of epithelial cell-type identity.
evidence: Inferred from pAKT expression patterns

claim: Shh-Cre x Pik3caf/f mice were used to conditionally delete the Pik3ca gene from the embryonic mouse lung epithelium.
source: To test the hypothesis that epithelial activation of PI3K signaling is required for normal differentiation and proximal-distal patterning of the lung epithelium, we used Shh-Cre x Pik3caf/f mice to conditionally delete the Pik3ca gene from the embryonic mouse lung epithelium (Harfe et al., 2004; Zhao et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harfe et al., 2004 and Zhao et al., 2006

claim: The lungs of Pik3ca cKO embryos at E18.5 were remarkably mispatterned, with abnormal cysts lined by NKX2.1+ epithelial cells scattered throughout the lungs.
source: The lungs of Pik3ca cKO embryos at E18.5 were remarkably mispatterned, with abnormal cysts lined by NKX2.1+epithelial cells scattered throughout the lungs (Figure 6), with the remainder of the lungs filled with simplified alveolar structures lined by increased numbers of SOX9+ lung epithelial cells (Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figures 6 and 7

claim: The remainder of the lungs in Pik3ca cKO embryos at E18.5 were filled with simplified alveolar structures lined by increased numbers of SOX9+ lung epithelial cells.
source: The lungs of Pik3ca cKO embryos at E18.5 were remarkably mispatterned, with abnormal cysts lined by NKX2.1+epithelial cells scattered throughout the lungs (Figure 6), with the remainder of the lungs filled with simplified alveolar structures lined by increased numbers of SOX9+ lung epithelial cells (Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: Supported by histological and immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figures 6 and 7

claim: A significant increase in the number of Sox9+ epithelial cells was only observed at E18.5 in Pik3ca cKO embryos.
source: A significant increase in the number of Sox9+ epithelial cells was only observed at E18.5; in fact, the mean proportion of epithelium expressing Sox9 at E12.5 and E14.5 was slightly lower in Pik3ca cKO embryos (although this did not reach statistical significance).
evidence: Supported by quantification of SOX9+ cells at multiple timepoints

claim: The mean proportion of epithelium expressing Sox9 at E12.5 and E14.5 was slightly lower in Pik3ca cKO embryos (although this did not reach statistical significance).
source: A significant increase in the number of Sox9+ epithelial cells was only observed at E18.5; in fact, the mean proportion of epithelium expressing Sox9 at E12.5 and E14.5 was slightly lower in Pik3ca cKO embryos (although this did not reach statistical significance).
evidence: Supported by quantification of SOX9+ cells at multiple timepoints

claim: No significant differences were observed in the number of proliferative epithelial cells in Pik3ca cKO embryos.
source: No significant differences were observed in the number of proliferative epithelial cells.
evidence: Supported by Ki67 quantification

claim: The persistence of SOX9+ epithelial progenitor cells through the end of fetal lung development in Pik3ca cKO embryos suggests persistence rather than proliferative expansion.
source: Taken together, these data suggest a persistence (rather than proliferative expansion) of the SOX9+epithelial progenitor cell population through the end of fetal lung development.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of increased proliferation despite increased SOX9+ cell numbers

claim: There was a marked reduction in the number of differentiated secretory and ciliated airway epithelial cells in Pik3ca cKO lungs.
source: One of the most dramatic aspects of the phenotype observed in Pik3ca cKO lungs was the marked reduction in the number of differentiated secretory and ciliated airway epithelial cells. (Figure 8)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy and qPCR shown in Figure 8

claim: There was a decrease in both the total number of SCGB1A1+ secretory cells, and the intensity of SCGB1A1 staining within individual cells in Pik3ca cKO lungs.
source: There was a decrease in both the total number of SCGB1A1+ secretory cells, and the intensity of SCGB1A1 staining within individuals cells, as measured by immunofluorescence microscopy. (Figure 8Y-MM, QQ)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 8Y-MM, QQ

claim: There was a dramatic reduction in the mRNA levels of the secretory cell markers Scgb1a1 and Scgb3a2 in Pik3ca cKO lungs.
source: Moreover, there was a dramatic reduction in the mRNA levels of the secretory cell markers Scgb1a1 and Scgb3a2. (Figure 8PP)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8PP

claim: There was a reduction in the total number of ciliated cells in Pik3ca cKO lungs.
source: A similar reduction was observed in the total number of ciliated cells, altered expression patterns of the microtubule protein TUB1A1, and a marked reduction on Foxj1 mRNA levels. (Figure Y-MM, NN-OO)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy and qPCR shown in Figure 8

claim: There was altered expression patterns of the microtubule protein TUB1A1 in Pik3ca cKO lungs.
source: A similar reduction was observed in the total number of ciliated cells, altered expression patterns of the microtubule protein TUB1A1, and a marked reduction on Foxj1 mRNA levels. (Figure Y-MM, NN-OO)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 8

claim: There was a marked reduction in Foxj1 mRNA levels in Pik3ca cKO lungs.
source: A similar reduction was observed in the total number of ciliated cells, altered expression patterns of the microtubule protein TUB1A1, and a marked reduction on Foxj1 mRNA levels. (Figure Y-MM, NN-OO)
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8NN-OO

claim: The impact on the number of SOX2+ airway epithelial cells in Pik3ca cKO lungs was much less dramatic than the impact on secretory and ciliated cells.
source: In contrast, the impact on the number of SOX2+ airway epithelial cells was much less dramatic.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy and qPCR

claim: From E12.5-E16.5, there appears to be a decrease in the number of airway branches in Pik3ca cKO lungs consistent with an impairment in branching morphogenesis.
source: From E12.5-E16.5, there appears to be a decrease in the number of airway branches consistent with an impairment in braching morphogenesis, also evident in H&E staining shown in Figure 6.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: At E18.5, Sox2 mRNA expression levels were overall decreased by an average of 30% in Pik3ca cKO lungs (but did not reach statistical significance).
source: At E18.5, Sox2 mRNA expression levels were overall decreased by an average of 30% (but did not reach statistical significance; Figure 8A–X, NN).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8NN

claim: There is a significant impairment of airway epithelial differentiation following epithelial-specific loss of PI3K signaling.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that there is a significant impairment of airway epithelial differentiation following epithelial-specific loss of PI3K signaling, with a more subtle impact on the total number of SOX2 +airway epithelial cells overall.
evidence: Inferred from the marked reduction in secretory and ciliated cells with less impact on SOX2+ cells

claim: Epithelial-specific PI3K signaling is required for proper proximal/distal patterning of the lung during development.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that epithelial-specific PI3K signaling is required for proper proximal/distal patterning of the lung during development.
evidence: Supported by the mispatterning phenotype observed in Pik3ca cKO mice

claim: Loss of PI3K signaling causes persistence of the SOX9+ lung epithelial progenitors into late embryonic life.
source: Both in vivo and in vitro data demonstrate that loss of PI3K signaling causes persistence of the SOX9+ lung epithelial progenitors into late embryonic life, inhibiting normal proximal lung epithelial differentiation and resulting in mispatterning of both the airway and alveolar structures of the lung.
evidence: Supported by in vivo experiments using Pik3ca cKO mice

claim: Loss of PI3K signaling inhibits normal proximal lung epithelial differentiation.
source: Both in vivo and in vitro data demonstrate that loss of PI3K signaling causes persistence of the SOX9+ lung epithelial progenitors into late embryonic life, inhibiting normal proximal lung epithelial differentiation and resulting in mispatterning of both the airway and alveolar structures of the lung.
evidence: Supported by in vivo experiments showing decreased secretory and ciliated cells

claim: Loss of PI3K signaling results in mispatterning of both the airway and alveolar structures of the lung.
source: Both in vivo and in vitro data demonstrate that loss of PI3K signaling causes persistence of the SOX9+ lung epithelial progenitors into late embryonic life, inhibiting normal proximal lung epithelial differentiation and resulting in mispatterning of both the airway and alveolar structures of the lung.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis of Pik3ca cKO lungs

claim: Careful comparative analysis using both chromatin accessibility and gene expression data provides higher sensitivity to identify novel regulators of development that may be unrecognized from expression data alone.
source: Finally, this requirement for PI3K signaling demonstrates that careful comparative analysis using both chromatin accessibility and gene expression data provides higher sensitivity to identify novel regulators of development that may be unrecognized from expression data alone.
evidence: Inferred from the identification of PI3K signaling through combined ATAC-Seq and RNA-Seq analysis

claim: The mature mammalian lung is composed of dozens of specialized cell types that are necessary to permit gas exchange and facilitate terrestrial life.
source: The mature mammalian lung is composed of dozens of specialized cell types that are necessary to permit gas exchange and facilitate terrestrial life (Morrisey and Hogan, 2010; Swarr and Morrisey, 2015; Basil et al., 2020; Basil and Morrisey, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple reviews

claim: Accessible chromatin regions identified in this study are highly correlated with histone post-translational modifications normally associated with active, functional cis-regulatory elements.
source: Accessible chromatin regions identified in our study are highly correlated with histone post-translational modificiations normally associated with active, functional cis-regulatory elements, and changes in the accessibility of these regions of chromain are associated with changes in developmental gene expression.
evidence: Supported by comparison with ENCODE ChIP-Seq data

claim: Changes in the accessibility of chromatin regions are associated with changes in developmental gene expression.
source: Accessible chromatin regions identified in our study are highly correlated with histone post-translational modificiations normally associated with active, functional cis-regulatory elements, and changes in the accessibility of these regions of chromain are associated with changes in developmental gene expression.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between ATAC-Seq and RNA-Seq data

claim: Changes in chromatin accessibility were preferentially located at putative enhancers, highlighting the importance of targeted chromatin remodeling at select enhancers in the development of the SOX9+ lung epithelial progenitors.
source: Changes in chromatin accessibility were preferentially located at putative enhancers, highlighting the importance of targeted chromatin remodeling at select enhancers in the development of the SOX9+ lung epithelial progenitors.
evidence: Inferred from the preferential location of DARs at intronic and intergenic regions

claim: The combinatorial approach to the analysis of both mRNA and chromatin accessibility data led to the observation that PI3K was a key regulator of EPC development.
source: Our combinatorial approach to the analysis of both mRNA and chromatin accessibility data led to the observation that PI3K was a key regulator of EPC development.
evidence: Supported by PECA and GSEA analyses of paired ATAC-Seq and RNA-Seq data

claim: Signaling through the PI3K pathway, as measured by pAKT immunostaining, was highest in the proximal lung epithelium throughout development.
source: Signaling through the PI3K pathway, as measured by pAKT immunostaining, was highest in the proximal lung epithelium throughout development.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy for pAKT

claim: A paucity of airways were observed in the Pik3ca cKO lungs.
source: In vivo, a paucity of airways were observed in the Pik3ca cKO lungs; although the airways present were lined by SOX2+ epithelium, mature secretory and ciliated cell markers were decreased.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis

claim: Although the airways present in Pik3ca cKO lungs were lined by SOX2+ epithelium, mature secretory and ciliated cell markers were decreased.
source: In vivo, a paucity of airways were observed in the Pik3ca cKO lungs; although the airways present were lined by SOX2+ epithelium, mature secretory and ciliated cell markers were decreased.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy and qPCR

claim: Pik3ca cKO mice demonstrated extensive distal cysts and simplified alveoli.
source: Pik3ca cKO mice also demonstrated extensive distal cysts and simplified alveoli.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis

claim: An intact gradient of PI3K signaling during development is needed for proper differentiation of the proximal and distal portions of the lung.
source: Both results emphasize the need for an intact gradient of PI3K signaling during development for proper differentiation of the proximal and distal portions of the lung.
evidence: Inferred from the mispatterning phenotype in Pik3ca cKO mice

claim: The role of PI3K signaling in directing branching morphogenesis remains incompletely defined.
source: The role of PI3K signaling in directing branching morphogenesis remains incompletely defined.
evidence: Stated as a gap in knowledge

claim: Conditional deletion of Pik3ca in the developing lung epithelium in vivo appears to lead to impaired branching morphogenesis.
source: Although conditional deletion of Pik3ca in the developing lung epithelium in vivo appears to lead to impaired branching morphogenesis, lung explant models employing pharmacologic inhibitors of PI3K signaling, and a recent study that conditionally deleted Pik3ca in the lung mesenchyme during mouse lung development show an increase in branching morphogenesis. (Carter et al., 2014; Dai et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by histological analysis of Pik3ca cKO lungs

claim: Lung explant models employing pharmacologic inhibitors of PI3K signaling show an increase in branching morphogenesis.
source: Although conditional deletion of Pik3ca in the developing lung epithelium in vivo appears to lead to impaired branching morphogenesis, lung explant models employing pharmacologic inhibitors of PI3K signaling, and a recent study that conditionally deleted Pik3ca in the lung mesenchyme during mouse lung development show an increase in branching morphogenesis. (Carter et al., 2014; Dai et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to Carter et al., 2014 and Dai et al., 2022

claim: A recent study that conditionally deleted Pik3ca in the lung mesenchyme during mouse lung development showed an increase in branching morphogenesis.
source: Although conditional deletion of Pik3ca in the developing lung epithelium in vivo appears to lead to impaired branching morphogenesis, lung explant models employing pharmacologic inhibitors of PI3K signaling, and a recent study that conditionally deleted Pik3ca in the lung mesenchyme during mouse lung development show an increase in branching morphogenesis. (Carter et al., 2014; Dai et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to Dai et al., 2022

claim: FGF signaling, particularly FGF7 and FGF10 signaling through FGFR1/2 has been shown to play a key role in initial outgrowth of the lung bud and subsequent branching morphogenesis.
source: FGF signaling, particularly FGF7 and FGF10 signaling through FGFR1/2 has been shown to play a key role in initial outgrowth of the lung bud and subsequent branching morphogenesis.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field

claim: Abrogation of FGF7 or FGF10 signaling through FGFR1/2 causes apoptosis and failure of lung epithelial outgrowth, not expansion of SOX9+ progenitor cells.
source: However, abrogation of FGF7 or FGF10 signaling through FGFR1/2 causes apoptosis and failure of lung epithelial outgrowth, not expansion of SOX9+ progenitor cells as observed presently, and thus the phenotypes observed in Pik3ca cKO animals cannot simply be explained by a downstream effector of the FGF7/10-FGFR1/2 signaling axis; EGF, other FGFs, and IGF are all potential regulators to be explored.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field

claim: The phenotypes observed in Pik3ca cKO animals cannot simply be explained by a downstream effector of the FGF7/10-FGFR1/2 signaling axis.
source: However, abrogation of FGF7 or FGF10 signaling through FGFR1/2 causes apoptosis and failure of lung epithelial outgrowth, not expansion of SOX9+ progenitor cells as observed presently, and thus the phenotypes observed in Pik3ca cKO animals cannot simply be explained by a downstream effector of the FGF7/10-FGFR1/2 signaling axis; EGF, other FGFs, and IGF are all potential regulators to be explored.
evidence: Inferred from the difference in phenotypes

claim: EGF, other FGFs, and IGF are all potential regulators of PI3K signaling in lung development to be explored.
source: However, abrogation of FGF7 or FGF10 signaling through FGFR1/2 causes apoptosis and failure of lung epithelial outgrowth, not expansion of SOX9+ progenitor cells as observed presently, and thus the phenotypes observed in Pik3ca cKO animals cannot simply be explained by a downstream effector of the FGF7/10-FGFR1/2 signaling axis; EGF, other FGFs, and IGF are all potential regulators to be explored.
evidence: Speculative based on known PI3K pathway components

claim: The PI3K pathway may regulate chromatin state during lung development.
source: Third, our data suggest that the PI3K pathway may regulate chromatin state during lung development.
evidence: Speculative based on the correlation between PI3K signaling and chromatin accessibility changes

claim: Studies from cancer have shown that pAKT can directly interact with a number of key chromatin regulatory (CR) complexes to modulate chromatin state.
source: Studies from cancer, where aberrant activation of PI3K signaling is common, have shown that pAKT can directly interact with a number of key chromatin regulatory (CR) complexes to modulate chromatin state (Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2019

claim: The PI3K signaling pathway may serve as the central 'switch-board' integrating signals received from diverse receptor ligand-pairs during lung epithelial development.
source: We speculate that the PI3K signaling pathway serves as the central 'switch-board' integrating signals received from diverse receptor ligand-pairs during lung epithelial development, and in turn directly modulates chromatin state, including chromatin accessibility, through interactions between pAKT and key CR complexes to direct lung epithelial differentiation (Figure 9).
evidence: Speculative model based on the data presented

claim: PI3K signaling may directly modulate chromatin state, including chromatin accessibility, through interactions between pAKT and key CR complexes to direct lung epithelial differentiation.
source: We speculate that the PI3K signaling pathway serves as the central 'switch-board' integrating signals received from diverse receptor ligand-pairs during lung epithelial development, and in turn directly modulates chromatin state, including chromatin accessibility, through interactions between pAKT and key CR complexes to direct lung epithelial differentiation (Figure 9).
evidence: Speculative model based on the data presented and shown in Figure 9

claim: It remains unknown which of the dozens of proteins and complexes that are known to remodel chromatin are specifically required for development and differentiation of the lung epithelium.
source: It remains unknown which of the dozens of proteins and complexes that are known to remodel chromatin are specifically required for development and differentiation of the lung epithelium.
evidence: Stated as a gap in knowledge

claim: Studies in other tissues imply that specific CR complexes interface with major developmental transcription factors to mediate chromatin accessibility.
source: Studies in other tissues imply that specific CR complexes interface with major developmental transcription factors to mediate chromatin accessibility, and that chromatin accessibility changes are an integral part of cell-type identity.
evidence: General knowledge from studies in other tissues

claim: Chromatin accessibility changes are an integral part of cell-type identity.
